title: The poem: a ghazel on the Mevlevi sema
greek: Arabic samāʿ ('listening', the musical ritual of the Sufis); Turkish semâ
short: A seven-couplet ghazel by Şeyh Galib on the sema, the turning ritual of the Mevlevi dervishes, in which the whole cosmos is seen to whirl with them.
body: Gibb printed this as Ghazel [408] in his History of Ottoman Poetry, the first of four ghazels he gave from Galib's Divan, noting that it refers to the sema, which led Europeans to call the Mevlevis 'Dancing' or 'Whirling Dervishes'. Galib (1757-1799) was born into a Mevlevi family, entered the order, and in 1791 became sheikh of the Galata Mevlevihane, where Sultan Selim III, himself a composer, rebuilt the semahane. The poem appears to be the seven-couplet ghazel with the refrain 'eyler semâ' ('performs the sema') on which Demirbağ (2024) has published a commentary, reading it as a picture of all existence drawn towards divine love.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (London: Luzac, 1905), Ghazel [408], pp. 203-204, with Gibb's notes
M. Muhsin Kalkışım, 'Şeyh Galib', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 39 (2010), pp. 54-57
Abdulsamet Demirbağ, 'A Commentary on Sheikh Galib's Ghazal with "Eyler Semâ" Rhymed', Bingöl Üniversitesi Sosyal Bilimler Enstitüsü Dergisi 27 (2024), pp. 122-128

title: The refrain
greek: Arabic radīf; Turkish redif; probably 'eyler semâ'
short: Every couplet ends with 'in mystic dance', Gibb's rendering of the ghazel's repeated end-phrase (redif), which ties each new image to the sema.
body: A ghazel keeps one rhyme and, often, a repeated word or phrase after the rhyme (redif) in both lines of the first couplet and the second line of every other. Gibb reproduces the effect with 'in mystic dance' and an English rhyme on '-ere' (here, sphere, appear, clear...). The refrain makes the ghazel itself turn: lovers, sun and moon, the heavens, the weeping eye, the tavern boys, the angels, Mecnun's birds and finally the Mevlevis are each caught up in the same motion. If the original redif is 'eyler semâ', as seems likely, each couplet literally ends 'performs the sema'.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (London: Luzac, 1905), pp. 203-204
Abdulsamet Demirbağ, 'A Commentary on Sheikh Galib's Ghazal with "Eyler Semâ" Rhymed', Bingöl Üniversitesi Sosyal Bilimler Enstitüsü Dergisi 27 (2024), pp. 122-128

title: The lovers: the dervishes
short: Gibb's note: 'The lovers are the Mevlevian dervishes'. In Sufi language the seeker of God is the lover and God the Beloved.
body: The Sufi vocabulary of love makes the dervish an âşık (lover) and God the ma'şûk (beloved). Gibb's note identifies the 'lovers' circling here as the Mevlevi dervishes performing the sema. The dervishes, the semazens, turn on their own axis, the right hand raised to receive grace and the left lowered to pass it on, while moving round the hall; the poem's next line makes the sun and moon do the same in their spheres. The ritual (also called mukabele) is the best-known form of Sufi sema.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (London: Luzac, 1905), p. 203, n. 3

anchor: Sun and moon traverse the sphere
title: Cosmic sema
short: As the dervishes turn, the sun and moon circle in their spheres: the ritual on earth mirrors the motion of the heavens.
body: Mevlevi tradition explained the sema as an imitation of the turning of the heavens and of all created things around their centre. Galib's couplet states the correspondence directly: the lovers in the hall and the planets in the sky perform the same dance. The idea that love moves the heavens is also old in philosophy (the heavens move out of desire for the First Mover), and English readers may compare the last line of Dante's Paradiso, 'the love that moves the sun and the other stars', though there is no direct link.

sources.cite: TDV contributor, 'Semâ', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 36 (2009), pp. 455-457

title: The secret of love
short: The hidden mystery of love set the heavens reeling, and all the worlds are still whirling from it.
body: Love (aşk) is in Sufi thought the cause of creation: the famous saying in which God says 'I was a hidden treasure and I wished to be known, so I created the world' was read as making love the motive of all existence. So the turning of the spheres is a kind of intoxication with that secret. Demirbağ's commentary, as summarized in its abstract, reads the ghazel as showing all existence drawn to divine love and links this attraction to the sema. 'All the worlds' (âlemler) are the many levels of being, from the earthly to the divine.

title: The weeping eye as whirlpool
short: The lover's weeping eye is a whirlpool that also turns, throwing up tears like pearls and spray.
body: Tears are pearls in the poetic code, and the eye that pours them is a sea or a spring. Galib adds motion: a whirlpool spins, so the weeping eye too 'dances'. The image shows his taste for joining stock figures in surprising ways, the hallmark of the 'Indian style' (sebk-i Hindî) of which he is the great Ottoman representative. Every couplet finds a new thing that turns.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (London: Luzac, 1905), p. 204
TDV contributor, 'Mazmun', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi

title: Young Magians round the Tavern, like pilgrims
short: The sweet tavern boys circle the Tavern as pilgrims circle the Kaaba: in Sufi code the tavern is the convent and its servants the dervishes.
body: In Persian and Turkish poetry the wine-tavern was imagined as kept by Zoroastrian 'Magians', whose young servants, the mugbeçe, poured wine; the Magian elder, pîr-i mugân, became a name for the Sufi master. Galib compares their circling to the pilgrims' tawaf, the sevenfold circumambulation of the Kaaba at Mecca. The daring parallel of tavern and Kaaba is a commonplace of Sufi poetry: the true pilgrimage is round the place where the wine of divine love is served. Gibb's 'in fere' is an old phrase meaning 'together, in company' (OED, s.v. 'fere').

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (London: Luzac, 1905), p. 204

title: The reed-flute
short: The ney, the Mevlevi reed-flute, plays; its sound recalls the opening of Rumi's Mesnevi, where the reed laments its separation from the reed-bed.
body: The ney is the central instrument of Mevlevi music, and its player (neyzen) leads the sema. Jalal al-Din Rumi's Mesnevi, the order's sacred book, opens with the complaint of the reed cut from its reed-bed, which became the emblem of the soul longing to return to its origin. When Galib says the reed 'thrills' in ecstasy, every Mevlevi reader would hear that opening. The ney's music is what sets the sema, and in the next line the angels, in motion.

title: The angels as birds
short: Gibb's note: the Heavenly Birds are the angels, so moved by the Mevlevi reed-flute that they too begin the sema, beating their wings like doves.
body: Gibb explains that the angels are meant, and that they are moved by the Mevlevian reed-flute to break into the sema themselves. Doves turning in flight over a courtyard are a familiar sight, and the beating of wings matches the spreading of the dervishes' skirts as they turn. The couplet moves the dance from the hall up to the heavens, completing the poem's vertical scheme of earth and sky.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (London: Luzac, 1905), p. 204, n. 1

title: Qays, that is Mecnun, with birds in his hair
greek: Arabic Qays; Majnūn ('possessed by jinn', mad)
short: The poet is Qays (Mecnun), the mad lover of Leylâ, in whose unkempt hair the desert birds built nests; now even the nests dance.
body: Qays ibn al-Mulawwah, called Mecnun ('madman'), loved Leylâ and, parted from her, wandered the desert with the wild beasts. Gibb's note recalls that the birds built their nests in his long unkempt hair. The story came to Ottoman readers through Nizami and through Fuzûlî's Turkish Leylâ vü Mecnûn (1535). Galib's twist is that the lover's ecstasy shakes his head so that the very nests on it 'leap and rear' in the dance. Gibb's 'whiles' is an old word for 'at times'.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (London: Luzac, 1905), p. 204, n. 2
TDV contributor, 'Leylâ vü Mecnûn', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi

title: The Sun of Love: a hint of Şems
short: While the Sun of Love pours out its light, the Mevlevis turn like motes in a sunbeam. 'Sun' may also recall Shams of Tabriz, Rumi's master.
body: The mote dancing in a sunbeam is one of Rumi's favourite images for the soul's ecstatic movement in the light of God. Shams-i Tabrizi ('Sun of Tabriz'), the wandering dervish whose friendship transformed Rumi in 1244, gave his name, which means 'sun', to a whole cycle of Rumi's lyrics. A Mevlevi poet saying 'Sun of Love' could hardly avoid the association, though the main sense is God as the source of love's light. The image ends the poem on the smallest and the greatest at once: the mote and the sun.

sources.cite: Annemarie Schimmel, Mystical Dimensions of Islam (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1975)

title: The Mevlevis
greek: Arabic mawlawī, from mawlānā ('our master', Rumi); Turkish Mevlevî
short: The final couplet names the Mevlevis, the Sufi order founded on Rumi's teaching, of which Galib was a sheikh.
body: The Mevlevi order takes its name from Mevlânâ ('our master'), Jalal al-Din Rumi (d. 1273), and was organized by his son Sultan Veled; its mother house is at Konya, and its convents (mevlevîhâne) were centres of music and poetry across the Ottoman lands. Galib, as sheikh of the Galata Mevlevihane from 1791, presided over its sema. In the signature couplet the poet names himself, 'Ghalib', and his order together, so that the ghazel ends with the community whose ritual it has described from the first line.
